question: Under North Dakota's Subdivided Lands Disposition Act, land qualifies as a "subdivision" subject to registration when it is located outside North Dakota and:
choice_a: Divided into any number of parcels regardless of size
choice_b: Located within North Dakota and divided into ten or more lots
choice_c: Divided or proposed to be divided into five or more lots, parcels, units, or interests for disposition (or offered as part of a common promotional plan involving five or more)
choice_d: Owned by a licensed North Dakota broker
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-02(7) defines "subdivision"/"subdivided lands" as land situated outside North Dakota divided (or proposed to be divided) for disposition into five or more lots, parcels, units, or interests, or any land (contiguous or not) if five or more are offered under a common promotional plan. Choice C is wrong because the land must be located OUTSIDE North Dakota, not within it, to fall under this Act.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-04, unless an exemption applies, it is unlawful for a person in North Dakota to do what regarding subdivided lands located outside the state?
choice_a: List the property with any out-of-state MLS
choice_b: Charge more than a 6% commission on the sale
choice_c: Advertise the property without commission approval of the price
choice_d: Offer or dispose of any interest in the subdivided lands before the lands are registered with the commission
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-04(1) makes it unlawful to offer or dispose of any interest in subdivided lands located outside North Dakota prior to registration of those lands. Choices A, C, and D describe conduct not addressed by this prohibition.

question: Besides registering the subdivided lands, what must occur before a person may lawfully dispose of an interest in registered subdivided lands to a North Dakota purchaser?
choice_a: A current public offering statement must be delivered to the purchaser, who must be given a reasonable opportunity to examine it before the disposition
choice_b: The purchaser must first obtain title insurance
choice_c: The purchaser must sign a waiver of the right to rescind
choice_d: The commission must personally interview the purchaser
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-04(2) prohibits disposition of subdivided lands unless a current public offering statement is delivered and the purchaser has a reasonable opportunity to examine it before the disposition. Choices A, B, and D describe no requirement found in this statute.

question: Which of the following dispositions is exempt from the Subdivided Lands Disposition Act's registration requirements, absent an intent to evade the chapter?
choice_a: A subdivider disposing of 50 lots to the general public through a promotional advertising campaign
choice_b: A purchaser reselling subdivided lands for that purchaser's own account in a single, isolated transaction
choice_c: A developer offering 20 lots as part of a common promotional plan
choice_d: A subdivider who has been convicted of land-sale fraud within the past ten years
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-05(1)(a) exempts a purchaser's own-account disposition of subdivided lands in a single or isolated transaction. Choices A and B describe exactly the mass-marketing scenarios the chapter targets; choice C describes a subdivider the commission could deny registration to under 43-23.1-08(4), not a statutory exemption.

question: A subdivider offers only three separate parcels of out-of-state land for disposition within a twelve-month period. Under NDCC 43-23.1-05, this offering is:
choice_a: Still subject to full registration because any offering of out-of-state land requires registration
choice_b: Exempt only if the subdivider is a licensed North Dakota broker
choice_c: Exempt from the Act's registration provisions, since fewer than five lots were offered in the twelve-month period
choice_d: Subject to registration only if the parcels exceed one acre each
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-05(1)(b) exempts offerings of fewer than five separate lots, parcels, units, or interests in a twelve-month period. Choice B ignores this numeric exemption; choices C and D describe conditions not found in the statute.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-05, the registration provisions of the Subdivided Lands Disposition Act generally do not apply to the sale or lease of:
choice_a: Any land parcel under five acres in size
choice_b: Land sold exclusively to relatives of the subdivider
choice_c: Land that has previously been registered in any other state
choice_d: Improved land with an existing residential, commercial condominium, or industrial building, or land under a contract obligating the seller to erect such a building within two years
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-05(3) exempts improved land already bearing a residential, commercial condominium, or industrial building, or land under a contract to have one erected within two years. Choices A, C, and D are not statutory exemptions.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-05(2)(b), the registration requirements of the Subdivided Lands Disposition Act do not apply to a subdivision if the plan of disposition is to dispose of the land to:
choice_a: Ten or fewer persons
choice_b: Twenty-five or fewer persons
choice_c: Any number of persons, so long as all are North Dakota residents
choice_d: Five or fewer government agencies
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-05(2)(b) exempts a subdivision where the plan of disposition is to dispose to ten or fewer persons. Choices A, B, and D do not match the statutory threshold.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-09, what is the registration fee for subdivided lands, and how long does a registration remain effective before renewal is required?
choice_a: A $500 fee, with registration effective for five years
choice_b: A $100 fee, with registration effective for one year and renewable annually for a further $100 fee
choice_c: No fee is required, but registration must be renewed monthly
choice_d: A $1,000 fee, with lifetime registration
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-09(1) sets the registration fee at $100, and 43-23.1-09(4) makes registration effective for one year, renewable annually with a nonrefundable $100 renewal fee. Choices A, B, and C misstate the fee and duration.

question: After the commission issues a notice of filing on a subdivided-lands registration application, what happens if the commission enters no order of rejection within ninety days?
choice_a: The application is automatically denied
choice_b: The applicant must resubmit a new application
choice_c: The land is deemed registered, unless the applicant has consented in writing to a delay
choice_d: The commission must refund the registration fee
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-09(1) provides that if no rejection order is entered within ninety days of the notice of filing, the land is deemed registered unless the applicant consented in writing to a delay. Choices B, C, and D are not consequences described in the statute.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-07, once subdivided lands are registered, how may the public offering statement be used for promotional purposes?
choice_a: It may be freely edited by the subdivider's sales staff to highlight favorable terms
choice_b: It may be replaced entirely by advertising brochures
choice_c: It is optional once the property is registered
choice_d: Only if used in its entirety — no portion may be underscored, italicized, or otherwise emphasized differently from the rest without commission approval
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-07(2) requires the public offering statement to be used in its entirety after registration and bars special typographic emphasis on any portion unless the commission requires it. Choices A, C, and D contradict this full-disclosure mandate.

question: As part of its examination of a subdivided-lands registration application, the commission must determine that the subdivider (or its officers/principals, if a business entity) has not been convicted of a crime involving land dispositions within what time period?
choice_a: The past ten years
choice_b: The past two years
choice_c: The past twenty years
choice_d: Ever, with no time limitation
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-08(4) requires the commission to confirm the subdivider has not been convicted of a land-disposition-related crime, or subjected to an injunction or administrative order for false or misleading promotion, within the past ten years. Choices A, B, and D misstate this lookback period.

question: As a condition of registering subdivided lands, NDCC 43-23.1-11 requires the subdivider to file an indemnity bond running to the State of North Dakota. What is the statutory minimum amount of this bond?
choice_a: Ten thousand dollars
choice_b: Twenty-five thousand dollars
choice_c: Fifty thousand dollars
choice_d: There is no statutory minimum; the commission sets the amount case by case
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-11(3) requires an indemnity bond in an amount the commission deems necessary to protect purchasers, "but in no event less than twenty-five thousand dollars." Choices A and B misstate the floor, and choice C is wrong because a statutory floor exists.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-17, who may lawfully offer or dispose of subdivided lands within or from North Dakota, outside of an exempt transaction?
choice_a: Any adult resident of North Dakota
choice_b: Only an attorney licensed to practice in North Dakota
choice_c: Only a real estate broker, salesperson, or mortgage broker licensed under chapter 43-23
choice_d: Only the subdivider personally, with no licensee involvement permitted
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-17 requires that no real estate broker, salesperson, or mortgage broker offer or dispose of subdivided lands unless licensed under chapter 43-23, except in exempt transactions. Choices B, C, and D do not reflect this licensing requirement.

question: If a disposition of subdivided lands is made in violation of the Subdivided Lands Disposition Act, NDCC 43-23.1-18 provides that the disposition is:
choice_a: Automatically void, with no purchaser election required
choice_b: Valid and unaffected, though the subdivider may face criminal charges
choice_c: Voidable only by the commission, not the purchaser
choice_d: Voidable at the election of the purchaser, entitling the purchaser to recover the consideration paid plus interest, taxes/assessments paid, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-18(1) makes a violative disposition voidable at the purchaser's election, with joint and several liability of the seller and participating agents for the consideration paid plus 6% interest, taxes/assessments, court costs, and attorney's fees. Choices A, C, and D misstate who controls the remedy and its effect.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-18(2), an action to recover consideration paid for an unlawfully disposed subdivided-land interest must be brought no later than:
choice_a: Five years from the date of disposition, or three years after the purchaser received information about the basis for recovery, whichever occurs first
choice_b: Ten years from the date of disposition, with no exceptions
choice_c: One year from the date of disposition only
choice_d: There is no limitations period for this civil remedy
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-18(2) sets the limitations period at five years from disposition or three years from the purchaser's discovery of the basis for recovery, whichever comes first. Choices A, B, and D misstate or omit this dual deadline.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.1-23, a person who willfully violates the Subdivided Lands Disposition Act, or a related commission rule or order, is guilty of:
choice_a: A class B misdemeanor
choice_b: A class C felony
choice_c: An infraction only
choice_d: A class A felony
explanation: NDCC 43-23.1-23 makes a willful violation of the chapter, or of a rule, regulation, or order under it, a class C felony — a notably more severe penalty than the class B misdemeanor for unlicensed practice under 43-23-17. Choices A, B, and C misstate the offense class.

question: Under North Dakota law, which license holder bears the explicit statutory duty to deliver a complete, detailed closing statement to the party or parties represented in every real estate transaction?
choice_a: Any real estate salesperson may deliver it directly without broker involvement
choice_b: Only the title company handling closing
choice_c: The broker only, since a salesperson acts under the broker's license and supervision
choice_d: Only the buyer's attorney, if one is retained
explanation: NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o) makes it grounds for discipline if "a broker" fails to deliver a complete detailed closing statement to the party or parties the broker represents — the duty runs to the broker. Choices B, C, and D are not the statutory duty-holder.

question: What must a North Dakota broker's closing statement, required under NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o), show?
choice_a: Only the total sale price, with no itemization
choice_b: Only the broker's commission amount
choice_c: Only disbursements to the seller, never receipts
choice_d: All of the receipts and disbursements handled by the broker for the party or parties the broker represents
explanation: NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o) requires the closing statement to show "all of the receipts and disbursements handled by the broker for the party or parties represented by the broker." Choices A, C, and D describe partial disclosures that would not satisfy this standard.

question: When must a North Dakota broker deliver the required closing statement to the party or parties the broker represents?
choice_a: At the time the transaction is consummated
choice_b: Within thirty days after the buyer moves in
choice_c: Only if the client requests it in writing
choice_d: At the time the listing agreement is signed
explanation: NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o) requires delivery "at the time the transaction is consummated." Choices A, B, and D do not match the statutory timing trigger.

question: Besides delivering the closing statement to the represented party, what additional recordkeeping obligation does NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o) impose on the broker?
choice_a: The broker must file the closing statement with the county recorder
choice_b: The broker must retain true copies of the closing statements in the broker's files
choice_c: The broker must forward the closing statement to the state real estate commission automatically
choice_d: The broker has no further obligation once the statement is delivered
explanation: NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o) requires the broker "to retain true copies of the statements in the broker's files," in addition to delivering the statement to the represented party. Choices A and B are not required by this provision, and choice C contradicts the express retention duty.

question: A North Dakota broker lawfully represents both the buyer and the seller in a transaction, with proper written agency agreements and disclosure. Under NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o), how does the broker's closing-statement duty apply?
choice_a: The broker need only provide a closing statement to whichever party paid the commission
choice_b: The closing statement requirement does not apply to dual-agency transactions
choice_c: The broker must deliver a complete detailed closing statement to the party or parties represented, which in this dual-agency transaction means both the buyer and the seller
choice_d: Only the seller receives a closing statement in a dual-agency transaction
explanation: The statute requires delivery to "the party or parties represented by the broker" — in a lawful dual-agency transaction, both parties are represented, so both must receive a complete detailed statement. Choices B, C, and D would leave a represented party without the disclosure the statute requires.
source_note: NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o); see also NDCC 43-23-06.1(6) (dual agency definition)

question: What is the consequence to a North Dakota broker who fails to deliver a complete, detailed closing statement as required by NDCC 43-23-11.1(1)(o)?
choice_a: The transaction is automatically voided
choice_b: The broker forfeits the earnest money to the buyer
choice_c: No consequence exists unless a client sues for damages
choice_d: It is grounds for commission discipline, which may include license suspension or revocation, a monetary fine, required course attendance, or a letter of reprimand
explanation: Failure to deliver the closing statement is listed among the grounds for discipline under NDCC 43-23-11.1(1), which authorizes the commission to suspend or revoke the license, impose a fine and costs, require course attendance, or issue a reprimand. Choices A, C, and D are not the statutory consequence.

question: What is the stated purpose of North Dakota's real estate education, research, and recovery fund under NDCC 43-23.2-01?
choice_a: To pay unsatisfied judgments to aggrieved persons and to fund education and research in real estate for licensees' benefit
choice_b: To pay the salaries of real estate commission staff
choice_c: To fund state-wide property tax relief for real estate purchasers
choice_d: To reimburse brokers for advertising expenses
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-01 creates the fund "to provide a fund whereby aggrieved persons may make application for the payment of unsatisfied judgments, and for the furnishing of education and research in the field of real estate for the benefit of licensees." Choices A, B, and D are not among the stated purposes.

question: Who administers North Dakota's real estate education, research, and recovery fund?
choice_a: The state treasurer independently
choice_b: The state real estate commission
choice_c: The North Dakota Insurance Department
choice_d: Each individual brokerage firm
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-01 specifies the fund "must be administered by the state real estate commission as provided within this chapter." Choices A, B, and C have no administrative role under this chapter.

question: How much must a person pay into the recovery fund the first time that person is licensed as a North Dakota real estate broker or salesperson, and how often is this fee paid?
choice_a: A $20 fee, paid with every annual renewal
choice_b: A $100 fee, paid once
choice_c: A $20 fee, paid only once, at first-time licensure
choice_d: No fee; the fund is financed solely by the state general fund
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-02(1) requires a first-time broker or salesperson licensee to pay a $20 fee into the fund at the time of obtaining the license, and this fee is paid "only once" (apart from any renewal assessment under subsection 2). Choice B misstates it as recurring; choices C and D misstate the amount or source.

question: If, as of June 30 of any year, the balance in the recovery fund falls below the statutory threshold, what happens under NDCC 43-23.2-02(2)?
choice_a: The commission must suspend all pending license renewals until the fund is replenished by the state legislature
choice_b: Only newly licensed brokers must pay a special assessment
choice_c: The fund is automatically closed and merged into the general licensing fee account
choice_d: Every licensed broker and salesperson must pay an additional renewal assessment, not to exceed $20, sufficient to restore the fund to at least $60,000
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-02(2) triggers an additional renewal-time assessment, up to $20 per licensee, whenever the June 30 balance drops below $60,000, sized to restore the fund to at least that amount. Choices A, C, and D do not reflect the statute's mechanism.

question: What minimum balance must the commission maintain in the recovery fund for recovery purposes under NDCC 43-23.2-02(3)?
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-02(3) requires the commission to "maintain a minimum of sixty thousand dollars in the fund for recovery purposes." $15,000 (choice A) is instead the per-transaction and per-licensee claim cap under 43-23.2-03 and 43-23.2-08, a distinct figure from the fund's minimum balance.

question: NDCC 43-23.2-02(5) requires the commission's executive director to furnish a bond related to the recovery fund. What amount must this bond be?
choice_a: $15,000, matching the per-claim cap
choice_b: $60,000, matching the fund's required minimum balance
choice_d: No bond is required of the executive director
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-02(5) requires the executive director to "furnish a bond in the amount of sixty thousand dollars, upon such conditions as the commission may prescribe" — mirroring the fund's statutory minimum balance. Choices A, B, and C misstate or deny this requirement.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.2-02(4), what may the commission do, in its discretion, with recovery-fund moneys in excess of the required $60,000 minimum?
choice_a: Distribute the excess as dividends to licensed brokers
choice_b: Transfer the excess to the state general fund
choice_c: Use the excess to promote real estate education and research, underwrite educational seminars, establish courses at North Dakota institutions of higher learning, or fund research projects
choice_d: The excess must remain untouched and cannot be used for any purpose
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-02(4) lists several education and research uses for excess fund moneys, regardless of whether the excess derives from fees or accrued interest. Choices B, C, and D are not authorized or required uses under the statute.

question: On what grounds may an aggrieved person seek payment from North Dakota's real estate recovery fund under NDCC 43-23.2-03?
choice_a: Any breach of contract claim against a licensee, regardless of the nature of the breach
choice_b: A dispute over the amount of a broker's commission
choice_c: Simple negligence in preparing a listing description
choice_d: A final judgment against a licensee arising from fraudulent, deceptive, or dishonest practices, or conversion of trust funds, in a licensed transaction
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-03 limits recovery-fund claims to a final judgment obtained "on grounds of fraudulent, deceptive, or dishonest practices, or conversion of trust funds" arising from a licensed act or transaction. Choices A, C, and D fall outside this narrow statutory basis.

question: What is the maximum amount payable from North Dakota's real estate recovery fund per transaction, "regardless of the number of persons aggrieved or parcels of real estate involved," under NDCC 43-23.2-03?
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-03 caps fund liability at "fifteen thousand dollars per transaction regardless of the number of persons aggrieved or parcels of real estate involved in the transaction." Choices A, B, and D are not the per-transaction cap.

question: NDCC 43-23.2-04 requires an aggrieved person applying for recovery-fund payment to make certain showings at a hearing. Which of the following is one of the required showings?
choice_a: That the person is a licensed real estate broker
choice_b: That the person is not the spouse of the judgment debtor, or the personal representative of that spouse
choice_c: That the person purchased the property with cash, not financing
choice_d: That the person has never previously filed a real estate complaint
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-04(1) requires the applicant to show they are not the debtor's spouse, or that spouse's personal representative — a limitation meant to prevent a licensee's own family from recovering against the fund for the licensee's misconduct. Choices A, B, and C are not required showings.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.2-04(7), an aggrieved person's application for recovery-fund payment must be filed within what time period after the judgment becomes final?
choice_a: Not more than thirty days
choice_b: Not more than five years
choice_c: Not more than one year
choice_d: There is no deadline once judgment is obtained
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-04(7) requires the application to be made "not more than one year after the judgment becomes final." Choices B, C, and D misstate this filing deadline.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.2-08, what is the maximum total liability of North Dakota's recovery fund for claims against any one licensee, regardless of how many aggrieved persons file claims against that licensee?
choice_a: $15,000 per claimant, with no aggregate cap
choice_b: $60,000 per licensee
choice_c: There is no per-licensee cap, only a per-transaction cap
choice_d: $15,000, to be distributed pro rata among valid claimants if their aggregate claims exceed that amount
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-08 caps the fund's liability "for any one licensee" at $15,000 total, to be distributed pro rata among valid claimants if that sum is insufficient to pay all claims in full. Choice A contradicts the aggregate nature of the cap; choice C misstates the figure (that is the fund's overall minimum balance, not the per-licensee cap); choice D ignores this express limitation.

question: If the commission pays a claim from the recovery fund on behalf of a North Dakota licensee, what happens to that licensee's license under NDCC 43-23.2-09?
choice_a: The license is automatically suspended upon the effective date of the court's payment order, and reinstatement requires full repayment to the fund plus 4% annual interest
choice_b: The license is permanently and irrevocably revoked with no path to reinstatement
choice_c: Nothing happens to the license; only a note is placed in the licensee's file
choice_d: The license is suspended only if the licensee also faces separate commission disciplinary charges
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-09 automatically suspends the licensee's license upon the effective date of the court's payment order and conditions reinstatement on full repayment of the amount paid, plus interest at 4% a year. Choice A overstates the consequence as revocation rather than suspension; choices B and D understate or mischaracterize it.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.2-09, does a licensee's discharge in bankruptcy relieve that licensee of the obligation to repay amounts the recovery fund paid on the licensee's behalf?
choice_a: Yes — bankruptcy discharge fully extinguishes the repayment obligation
choice_b: No — a discharge in bankruptcy does not relieve the person from the penalties and disabilities provided in the chapter
choice_c: Yes, but only if the bankruptcy is a Chapter 7 filing
choice_d: The statute is silent on the effect of bankruptcy
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-09 expressly states that "a discharge in bankruptcy does not relieve a person from the penalties and disabilities provided in this chapter," preserving the repayment obligation. Choices A, B, and C contradict or ignore this express carve-out.

question: Under NDCC 43-23.2-10, if fund moneys allocated for purposes other than education and research are insufficient to pay a duly authorized claim at the time it is approved, how is the claim eventually satisfied?
choice_a: On a first-come, first-served basis determined by the size of the claim, largest first
choice_b: The claim is permanently denied if funds are insufficient at approval
choice_c: In the order the claims (or portions) were originally filed, once sufficient money has been deposited, plus accumulated interest at 4% a year
choice_d: Claims are satisfied by lottery among pending claimants
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-10 requires the commission to satisfy unpaid claims or portions "in the order that such claims or portions thereof were originally filed," plus 4% annual accumulated interest, once sufficient funds exist. Choices B, C, and D misstate this priority mechanism.

question: Does payment of a claim from the recovery fund, or a licensee's full repayment of that claim, limit the commission's authority to pursue separate disciplinary action against the licensee under NDCC 43-23.2-13?
choice_a: Yes — repayment in full automatically clears any related disciplinary proceeding
choice_b: Yes — the commission may not discipline a licensee who has been ordered to pay from the fund
choice_c: The statute does not address the interaction between fund payment and discipline
choice_d: No — the fund provisions do not limit the commission's authority to take disciplinary action under other provisions of chapter 43-23, and repayment does not nullify any separate disciplinary proceeding
explanation: NDCC 43-23.2-13 explicitly preserves the commission's separate disciplinary authority under chapter 43-23, regardless of fund payment or full repayment. Choices A, C, and D all misstate this express non-limitation.
